name: Separatist dissent from the established church
description: English Separatists formed dissenting churches outside the established Church of England. The relationship developed over time; 1534 is the royal-supremacy milestone, not a verified date for this Separatist split. The legacy record ID is retained for stable references.
narrative: English Separatists formed dissenting churches outside the established Church of England. The relationship developed over time; 1534 is the royal-supremacy milestone, not a verified date for this Separatist split. The legacy record ID is retained for stable references. Separatists went beyond Puritans who hoped to reform the national church from within. They formed dissenting communities, sometimes fled to the Netherlands, and developed different forms of church order. Smyth and Helwys belong to the part of this story that became Baptist; the wider movement also fed Congregational and Plymouth traditions. The existing 1606 date marks the immediate early-seventeenth-century Baptist context, not the beginning of all English Separatism.

name: Separatist exile congregation
description: English Separatists formed the first Baptist church in Amsterdam in 1609.
narrative: English Separatists formed the first Baptist church in Amsterdam in 1609. After leaving England for Amsterdam, Smyth’s congregation reconsidered whether infant baptism could constitute a church of professing believers. Around 1609 Smyth baptized himself and fellow members. Contact with Waterlander Mennonites then raised questions about that act and about the nature of a true church. Smyth sought Mennonite fellowship; Helwys opposed that course and eventually returned to England. The congregation’s importance lies in this contested process rather than a fully settled later Baptist system.

name: Baptist tradition begins
description: The Amsterdam congregation is treated as the first Baptist church, marking the start of the Baptist movement.
narrative: The Amsterdam congregation is treated as the first Baptist church, marking the start of the Baptist movement. English dissenters sought churches whose membership rested on professed faith rather than residence in a parish. Smyth and Helwys established an early Baptist congregation in Amsterdam around 1609; Helwys returned to England around 1612. Later Particular Baptists developed another influential English stream. General and Particular Baptists differed over salvation and election, and subsequent migration, missions, revival, and Black church organization produced many separate conventions. Baptist identity therefore describes a family, not one governing institution.
